evidence.claim: An Army supply corridor links forts and a Civil War battlefield.
evidence.quote: The Frontier Military Historic Byway follows a 19 th -century trail used by the Army to transport soldiers and supplies across eastern Kansas

evidence.claim: The Frontier Military Historic Byway crosses eastern Kansas on a mix of state highways, US highways and Interstate 435, linking Leavenworth with the Oklahoma border.
evidence.quote: Keep driving south along US-69 to U.S. Highway 69 Alternate, then on to the byway’s end at the Kansas/Oklahoma border.

evidence.claim: Kansas Tourism gives the historic byway’s length as 168 miles and highlights its forts and Civil War cavalry battlefield.
evidence.quote: Driving Directions Distance: 168 Miles

evidence.claim: At Fort Scott, the drive reaches the Osage Plains beside the Marmaton River.
evidence.quote: Fort Scott lies on the Osage Plains on the south side of the Marmaton River.

evidence.claim: The military road was built between 1838 and 1844 to carry soldiers and supplies among Fort Leavenworth, Fort Scott and Fort Gibson.
evidence.quote: The byway closely follows a road originally built between 1838 and 1844 that was used to transport soldiers and supplies from Fort Leavenworth in Kansas to Fort Scott in Kansas and to Fort Gibson in Oklahoma.

evidence.claim: Fort Scott was established on that road in 1842.
evidence.quote: In 1842, Fort Scott was named after Winfield Scott, was established on the American frontier on the military road in eastern Kansas between Fort Leavenworth and Fort Gibson.

evidence.claim: After the Army abandoned the post in 1853, its buildings were auctioned to settlers; during the Civil War it became a headquarters, supply depot and training center.
evidence.quote: After the army abandoned the fort in 1853, the buildings were purchased by local settlers at a government auction in 1855.

evidence.claim: Starting near Fort Leavenworth’s gates, follow K-7 south to K-5, then I-435 south and east to US 69.
evidence.quote: Beginning at the intersection of K-7 and K-92 near the gates of Fort Leavenworth in Leavenworth, KS, head south on K-7 towards K-5.

evidence.claim: Farther south, Mine Creek Battlefield lies southwest of Pleasanton, followed by Fort Scott on US 69.
evidence.quote: located 2.5 miles (4.0 km) southwest of Pleasanton in eastern Kansas

evidence.claim: US 69 Alternate reaches Baxter Springs on the Spring River before the byway ends at the Oklahoma line.
evidence.quote: Baxter Springs is sited on the western bank of the Spring River at the edge of the Ozarks, in the Spring River basin. U.S. Route 69 Alternate and U.S. Route 166 have a junction at the city

evidence.claim: on a mix of state highways, US highways and Interstate 435
evidence.quote: Drive south, then east along I-435 for an additional 30 miles and take the exit for US Highway 69.

evidence.claim: highlights its forts and Civil War cavalry battlefield.
evidence.quote: Learn and reflect at the site of one of the largest cavalry battles of the Civil War. Be transported in time at historical forts along the route.

evidence.claim: during the Civil War it became a headquarters, supply depot and training center.
evidence.quote: During the Civil War, Fort Scott was a U.S. Army district Headquarters, quartermaster supply depot, training center, and recruitment station.

evidence.claim: follow K-7 south to K-5, then I-435 south and east to US 69.
evidence.quote: Turn left onto K-5 and c ontinue south on K-5 for roughly 10 miles until you reach the entrance ramp for I-435. Drive south, then east along I-435 for an additional 30 miles and take the exit for US Highway 69.

evidence.claim: Fort Scott on US 69.
evidence.quote: Located at the intersection of U.S. Routes 54 and 69 in southeastern Kansas

evidence.claim: Colonel Henry Leavenworth and soldiers of the 3rd Infantry established this post in 1827 to protect the Santa Fe Trail.
evidence.quote: Colonel Henry Leavenworth, with the officers and men of the 3rd Infantry Regiment from Jefferson Barracks at St. Louis, Missouri, established Fort Leavenworth in 1827 to be a forward base protecting the Santa Fe Trail.

evidence.claim: It later supplied the Army of the West during the Mexican–American War.
evidence.quote: Throughout the Mexican–American War, Fort Leavenworth was the outfitting post for the Army of the West.

evidence.claim: The African-American 10th Cavalry Regiment formed here in 1866.
evidence.quote: Fort Leavenworth was also the base of African-American soldiers of the U.S. 10th Cavalry Regiment of the United States Army, formed on 21 September 1866 at Fort Leavenworth.

evidence.claim: A cavalry-rider statue honors the Buffalo Soldiers of the 9th and 10th Cavalry.
evidence.quote: Today, a statue of a cavalry rider stands at Fort Leavenworth in tribute to the "Buffalo Soldier" of the 9th and 10th Cavalry Regiments.

evidence.claim: Military education became another lasting role: the school William T. Sherman established in 1881 developed into the Army’s Command and General Staff College.
evidence.quote: In 1881, Gen. William T. Sherman established the School of Application for Cavalry and Infantry. That school evolved into the U.S. Army Command and General Staff College.

evidence.claim: A wagon train stalled at a creek crossing made retreating Confederate troops vulnerable at Mine Creek.
evidence.quote: After Marais des Cygnes, the Confederates fell back, but were stalled at the crossing of Mine Creek while a wagon train attempted to cross.

evidence.claim: Sterling Price’s army had withdrawn into Kansas after its defeat at Westport on October 23, 1864.
evidence.quote: After being defeated at Westport near Kansas City on October 23, Price's army began to retreat south through Kansas.

evidence.claim: Two days later, Union cavalry under John F. Philips and Frederick W. Benteen caught up at the crossing and defeated the defenders.
evidence.quote: Union cavalry commanded by Colonel John F. Philips and Lieutenant Colonel Frederick W. Benteen caught up to Price's army while it was stalled at the creek crossing.

evidence.claim: Confederate general John S. Marmaduke was among those captured.
evidence.quote: Many Confederate soldiers were captured, including Marmaduke.

evidence.claim: Preservation followed much later: Kansas legislators approved a 160-acre battlefield purchase in 1970, and a visitor center opened in 1998.
evidence.quote: In 1970, the Kansas legislature approved the acquisition of a 160-acre (65 ha) parcel of the battlefield area.

evidence.claim: Two days later
evidence.quote: The Battle of Mine Creek, also known as the Battle of Little Osage, was fought on October 25, 1864

evidence.claim: and defeated the defenders.
evidence.quote: Confederate cavalry commanded by Major General James F. Fagan and Brigadier General John S. Marmaduke attempted to defend against the Union assault, but were soundly defeated.

evidence.claim: a visitor center opened in 1998.
evidence.quote: A visitor center opened on October 24, 1998

evidence.claim: Fort Scott was built without defensive walls: open ground and available artillery made an enclosure unnecessary.
evidence.quote: Unlike most forts for military use, the fort did not have defensive walls or structures when first built; the wide-open area and the available artillery made an enclosed fort unnecessary.

evidence.claim: Its soldiers instead built quarters and structures for animals and equipment along a 350-foot parade ground.
evidence.quote: The soldiers concentrated on building structures for lodging the men, animals, and equipment. These buildings were on the edges of a 350-foot (110 m) parade ground.

evidence.claim: Captain Thomas Swords, the quartermaster, struggled with shortages of skilled labor, timber and equipment.
evidence.quote: Swords found his efforts plagued by lack of wood, skilled labor and working equipment.

evidence.claim: The post later recruited and trained Black soldiers for the Union Army during the Civil War.
evidence.quote: Fort Scott was one of the few installations that recruited and trained black soldiers for the United States Colored Troops of the Union Army.

evidence.claim: The National Park Service preserves the structures, parade ground and tallgrass prairie as witnesses to the fort’s 1842–1873 history.
evidence.quote: Each of these stories is a link in the chain of events that encircled Fort Scott from 1842-1873. All of the site's structures, its parade ground, and its tallgrass prairie bear witness to this era

evidence.claim: Notice the parade ground and restored tallgrass prairie at the historic site.
evidence.quote: The current national historic site protects 20 historic structures, a parade ground, and five acres (20,000 m2) of restored tallgrass prairie

evidence.claim: Captain Thomas Swords, the quartermaster
evidence.quote: The post quartermaster, Captain Thomas Swords, was in charge of building Fort Scott's structures

evidence.claim: Leavenworth sits on the Missouri River’s west bank; farther south, Pittsburg occupies an Ozark Highlands landscape of prairie and forest.
evidence.quote: The city lies on the west bank of the Missouri River in the Dissected Till Plains region of North America's Central Lowlands.

evidence.claim: Pittsburg occupies an Ozark Highlands landscape of prairie and forest.
evidence.quote: Pittsburg sits in the Ozark Highlands region, a mix of prairie and forests.

evidence.claim: Baxter Springs stands at the western edge of the Ozarks.
evidence.quote: Baxter Springs is sited on the western bank of the Spring River at the edge of the Ozarks

evidence.claim: The fort remains a United States Army installation within the city of Leavenworth, Kansas.
evidence.quote: Fort Leavenworth () is a United States Army installation located in Leavenworth County, Kansas, in the city of Leavenworth.

evidence.claim: Marked trails identify significant features of the battlefield for visitors.
evidence.quote: Marked trails are present at the site, allowing visitors to view the significant features of the battlefield.

evidence.claim: Officials halted further construction in 1850; the Army abandoned the post three years later in favor of Fort Riley farther west.
evidence.quote: officials decided on April 25, 1850, that no more construction would be done there, after eight years and $35,000. By the time it was finished, it was obsolete; three years later, it was abandoned by the military in favor of the more western Fort Riley.

flags: Kansas Tourism calls this a Historic Byway. Catalog scenic classification is not repeated. Route follows the old military corridor; no claim that modern pavement is the original road. Driving order is north to south, matching strip miles.
Drive-character evidence mainly describes the highway sequence and regional terrain; no supported travel time, grades or detailed roadside landscape is available.

Mine Creek sources conflict: battlefield page gives approximately 2,800 against about 8,000 in its opening, but less than 2,500 against about 7,000 later; battle page gives about 2,500–2,600 against an estimated 7,000. Removed published counts and the only-major-battle superlative.

Dropped oldest permanent settlement claim: Fort Leavenworth page uses that wording, but Kansas Territory narrows it to first permanent European settlement. Omitted rather than erase prior Indigenous settlement. The fort as the sole reason for the road is also omitted as unsupported.
Baxter tavern history is supported in its cache but omitted to focus the overview on the road’s construction and changing military role.

No Army visitor-access requirements are supplied. Fort Leavenworth’s continued military use does not establish unrestricted access, and no admission promise is made. Fort Scott prose does not imply all surviving structures are unaltered originals.
Mine Creek marked trails are described only in a secondary cache source; no current site-manager access page is available.
